title: Retinitis Pigmentosa: Comprehensive Clinical Roadmap
summary: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) represents a genetically heterogeneous group of progressive rod-cone dystrophies characterized by the primary degeneration of photoreceptor cells and the retinal pigment epithelium. This masterclass poster details the pathophysiology, diagnostic gold standards, and the current landscape of gene-based therapeutics.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is the most common hereditary retinal dystrophy, affecting approximately 1 in 4,000 individuals worldwide. It is defined by the progressive loss of rod photoreceptor function, followed by cone degeneration. The condition may be isolated (nonsyndromic) or part of a multi-system syndrome. Pathologically, it involves apoptosis of photoreceptors and the migration of RPE cells into the inner retina, forming the classic bone-spicule patterns.

sections.title: The Classic Diagnostic Triad
content: 1. Arteriolar Attenuation: Significant narrowing of retinal vessels.
2. Bone-Spicule Pigmentation: Perivascular pigment migration in the mid-periphery.
3. Waxy Disc Pallor: Reactive gliosis covering the optic nerve head.

sections.title: Progression of Symptoms
content: 1. Nyctalopia: Difficulty adapting to darkness (Rod dysfunction).
2. Peripheral Field Loss: Development of mid-peripheral scotomas.
3. Tunnel Vision: Constriction of visual fields to <20 degrees.
4. Central Loss: Eventual cone involvement or CME development.
5. Total Blindness: Often occurs in later decades, depending on genotype.

rows: Rapid onset, recoverin antibodies (+), normal fundus early
Central vision lost first, photophobia, bull's eye maculopathy

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME); occurs in 10-50% of patients.
Posterior Subcapsular Cataracts (PSC) are highly prevalent in RP.
High myopia is frequently associated with XLRP.
FAF 'Ring of Fire' correlates with the edge of the functional visual field.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Sudden vision loss (Rule out CME or Macular Hole)
Systemic weakness or cardiac issues (Think Kearns-Sayre Syndrome)
Polydactyly or obesity in a child (Think Bardet-Biedl)
Hearing loss (Screen for Usher Syndrome immediately)

branches: Refsum Disease (Phytanic acid buildup, Ataxia, Anosmia)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management Protocol
content: 1. Baseline Testing: Complete ERG, VF, OCT, and Genetic Testing.
2. Systemic Screening: Pediatric patients must have hearing tests and metabolic screens.
3. Pharmacotherapy: Consider Vitamin A Palmitate (15,000 IU/day) for adults (Berson Study).
4. Monitor Complications: Treat CME with topical/oral Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs).
5. Surgical Intervention: Cataract surgery (careful with zonular laxity) or Luxturna if RPE65 positive.
6. Low Vision Rehabilitation: Prisms, magnifiers, and mobility training.

sections.title: The Genetic Revolution: Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec-rzyl)
content: Mechanism: Adeno-associated virus (AAV2) vector delivering a functional RPE65 gene.
Eligibility: Confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations and sufficient viable retinal cells.
Delivery: Subretinal injection via pars plana vitrectomy.
Significance: First FDA-approved gene therapy for an inherited disease.

sections.title: Surgical Complications in RP Patients
content: Zonular Weakness: High risk of phacodonesis or late IOL dislocation.
CME Flare-up: Post-operative inflammation can worsen macular edema.
Epiretinal Membranes: Increased incidence in RP cases.
Capsular Opacification: Accelerated PCO formation is common.

sections.title: Future Frontiers & Research
content: Optogenetics: Turning remaining retinal cells into photoreceptors.
CRISPR/Cas9: In-vivo gene editing for specific mutations (e.g., CEP290).
Stem Cell Therapy: RPE and photoreceptor replacement.
Artificial Vision: Advanced retinal implants and cortical stimulators.
